subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Expectations as Reference Points
description: One-minute skill: Expectations as Reference Points.

hook.text: A restaurant with five stars on Yelp disappoints. A diner with two stars delights. Expectations set the bar.

buildup.text: Koszegi and Rabin argued that our reference point is whatever we recently expected to happen.

discovery.text: Expectations form a mental anchor. Every outcome is judged as better or worse than what we anticipated.

twist.text: Under-promise and over-deliver works because it sets a low reference point. Anything above it feels like a win.

climax.text: Managing others' expectations is managing their reference points. Lower the bar and then clear it.

punchline.text: Set expectations low. Then exceed them.

quiz.question: Why does under-promising and over-delivering work?
options: It sets a low reference point, making the outcome feel like a gain

details.summary: People evaluate outcomes not against zero but against what they expected to happen. When expectations serve as reference points, identical outcomes feel like gains or losses depending on whether they exceed or fall short of what was anticipated.
details.whyItMatters: Managing expectations is as important as managing reality. A company that beats low expectations gets rewarded more than one that misses high expectations, even if the second company performed better objectively.
takeaways: Expectations set the reference point against which outcomes are judged
Exceeding expectations feels like a gain even if the outcome is modest
Falling short of expectations feels like a loss even if the outcome is good

faq.question: Why do companies try to set low earnings expectations?
faq.answer: By guiding analyst expectations lower, companies create a reference point they can beat. Reporting earnings above expectations feels like a positive surprise, even if the actual numbers are mediocre. It is reference point manipulation.

faq.question: How do expectations affect consumer satisfaction?
faq.answer: A restaurant that slightly exceeds low expectations delights customers more than a fine dining establishment that slightly misses high expectations. Satisfaction depends on the gap between expectation and reality, not absolute quality.
